column1: What physical fact makes the 12th fret produce the exact octave of an open string?
column2: The 12th fret is the exact halfway point of the scale length, halving the vibrating string length and doubling the frequency (the octave).

column1: How does picking position near the bridge (ponticello) versus near the neck (tasto) affect tone, and why?
column2: Picking position filters harmonics by suppressing whichever harmonic has a node at that point. Near the bridge: bright, nasal, cutting tone. Near the neck: warm, flutey, fewer highs.

column1: Why does fretting a string typically sharpen its pitch, and what corrects this?
column2: Fretting stretches the string slightly, raising pitch a few cents. Saddle compensation (moving the saddle slightly back from theoretical scale length) corrects this per string.

column1: On an electric guitar bridge, which direction do you turn saddle screws to lower action, and what is the safe adjustment increment?
column2: Turn clockwise to lower action, counter-clockwise to raise it, in quarter-turn increments per saddle — recheck measurements after every adjustment, never stacking more than two turns before measuring.

column1: On an acoustic guitar, how does sanding material off the saddle base translate to change in 12th-fret action?
column2: It's roughly a 1:1 ratio — removing 0.3 mm of material from the saddle base lowers 12th-fret action by approximately 0.3 mm (unlike the nut, which is not 1:1).

column1: What defines a 'string set triad' and how many such shapes exist per triad quality on guitar?
column2: A string set triad is a close-position triad distributed across three adjacent strings. With 4 natural string sets (E-A-D, A-D-G, D-G-B, G-B-E) and 3 inversions each, there are 12 shapes per triad quality before octave displacement.

column1: What are the root-to-third, third-to-fifth, and root-to-fifth semitone intervals of a major triad?
column2: Major triad: Root to Third = 4 semitones (M3), Third to Fifth = 3 semitones (m3), Root to Fifth = 7 semitones (P5).

column1: What intervallic structure distinguishes a diminished triad from a minor triad?
column2: Diminished: m3 + m3 = diminished 5th (6 semitones) root to fifth. Minor: m3 + M3 = perfect 5th (7 semitones) root to fifth. The diminished triad's fifth is flatted by one semitone compared to minor.

column1: Why does the same chord shape on guitar NOT transpose uniformly in fret-number terms the way it would on a uniform-interval instrument?
column2: The guitar's tuning is asymmetric: four intervals of a perfect 4th (5 semitones) between most adjacent strings, but a major 3rd (4 semitones) between the G and B strings — this breaks shape uniformity across string sets.

column1: What is the Whole-Whole-Half-Whole-Whole-Whole-Half (W-W-H-W-W-W-H) pattern, and why is a scale shape learned at one fret reusable at any fret?
column2: It's the interval pattern of the major scale. Because equal temperament makes each fret a fixed semitone ratio, a scale shape sounds and functions identically regardless of which fret you start it on — one fingering works in all twelve keys.

column1: What is the key conceptual relationship between D Dorian and C Ionian, despite both using identical pitches?
column2: They share the same seven notes but measure them against different root/tonal centers: C Ionian treats C as home (major 3rd, major 6th above root), while D Dorian treats D as home (minor 3rd, major 6th above root), producing different emotional color from identical pitch content.

column1: In classical guitar seated position, what two posture elements prevent fretting-hand tension and strain?
column2: The neck is angled upward at roughly 45°, and the left elbow hangs freely with the wrist naturally aligned to the neck — no forced bend at the shoulder or wrist.
